title: Running Kth Highest Score
statement:
A leaderboard receives scores one at a time. After each new score it must report the k-th highest score so far.

  • KthLargest(k, nums) starts the board with the scores in nums.
  • add(val) records the score val and returns the k-th highest of all scores recorded so far.

Rank counts every copy: with scores [9, 9, 4] the 2nd highest is 9. nums may hold one score fewer than k, but after every add there are at least k scores.

Tests are written as a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the board. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: A low score like 10 cannot change the top three. The second 80 counts as its own entry, so the third highest jumps to 80.
The board starts one short of k. The first add fills it, and the answer can be lower than every starting score.

hints: Sorting everything after each add works but repeats a lot of work. Of all the scores, which ones can ever be the answer again?
Once a score has k higher-or-equal scores above it, it can never become the k-th highest again, because scores only get added. So you only need to keep the top k.
Keep the top k scores in a min-heap. Its smallest element, the root, is the k-th highest. On add, push the new score, and if the heap holds more than k, pop the smallest.

explain.intuition:
Scores only arrive, they never leave. So once a score is below the current top k, it can never climb back into the top k. That means you only need to remember the top k scores, and the answer is the smallest of them. You need a container that can quickly give you its smallest item, drop it, and take a new one. That is a min-heap.

A heap is a binary tree packed into an array: the children of index i sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and every parent is ≤ its children, so the minimum is always at index 0. The tree is complete, so its height is about log₂ n. Push puts the new item at the end and swaps it upward while it is smaller than its parent. Pop moves the last item to the root and swaps it downward with its smaller child. Each walks a single root-to-leaf path, so both cost O(log n), and reading the minimum is O(1). The heap is not fully sorted, and that is the point: it only does the work needed to keep the minimum on top. Python ships this as heapq, which works on a plain list. JavaScript and TypeScript have no heap, so you write a small class.
steps: In the constructor, push every starting score into a min-heap, popping whenever its size goes above k.
If the heap now holds more than k scores, pop the smallest. It can never be in the top k again.
Return the heap's root: the smallest of the top k, which is the k-th highest overall.
pitfalls: Using a max-heap of all scores. The k-th largest is then buried k levels of pops deep.
Not trimming the starting nums to k. If the heap keeps all of them, its root is the overall minimum, not the k-th highest.
Skipping a new score whenever it is not above the root, even while the heap still holds fewer than k scores. Example 2 needs the 3 to be kept.

complexity.time: O(n log k) to build, O(log k) per add

solutions.title: Sort after every add
solutions.idea: Keep every score in an array. After each add, sort it in descending order and read index k − 1.

solutions.title: Min-heap of the top k
solutions.idea: Keep only the k highest scores in a min-heap. The root is the answer, and anything that falls out of the heap can never return.

followups: Scores can now also be removed from the board. Why does the top-k heap stop working, and what structure would you use instead?
Report the k-th highest among only the last m scores, a sliding window. What changes?
